quote: (Aufstellung eines geeigneten allgemeinen Kriteriums dafür, dass ein Syst. ein wirklich bestimmtes ist!)
english: (Establishing a suitable general criterion for a system to be a genuinely determined one!)
topic: Hilbert discusses when a system of partial differential equations (including a Jacobian-type determinant condition) is genuinely determined, proposes finding a general criterion for this, and then sketches a plan to prove his independence theorem in the calculus of variations by deriving a partial differential equation for the minimum as a function of the endpoint.

triage.modern_statement: Find a general, checkable criterion for when a system of partial differential equations (possibly nonlinear, here including a Jacobian-determinant condition) is genuinely 'determined'. That means it is neither underdetermined (solutions depend on arbitrary functions beyond the expected Cauchy data) nor overdetermined (it has hidden integrability or compatibility conditions). In modern terms this is the problem of formal integrability and involutivity: deciding whether the system can be completed to an involutive form, and so whether it has a well-posed analytic initial value problem of Cauchy–Kovalevskaya type and what the 'size' of its general solution is (Cartan characters, Hilbert polynomial). The second half of the note, the independence-theorem plan, is a separate calculus-of-variations sketch and is not treated as an open problem here.
triage.answered_by: This was not answered as a reply to Hilbert's note. The general question was settled by the theory of formal integrability and involution: Riquier (c. 1910) and Janet (1920s) for analytic PDE systems, Élie Cartan and later Kähler for exterior differential systems (Cartan–Kähler theorem), and Spencer, Goldschmidt and others in the 1960s for a coordinate-free criterion via Spencer cohomology. Hilbert himself returned to a related theme for underdetermined systems in 'Über den Begriff der Klasse von Differentialgleichungen' (Math. Ann. 73, 1912), which Cartan answered.

evidence.claim: Riquier's method, developed further by Janet, and Cartan's approach, generalized by Kähler to exterior differential systems, give involutive completion. Involutive form lets one pose a well-defined initial value problem and removes hidden integrability conditions.
Maurice Janet's algorithms for systems of linear PDEs build on Riquier and decide the completeness/compatibility of PDE systems.
D. C. Spencer's 1969 survey 'Overdetermined systems of linear partial differential equations' (Bull. AMS 75) includes a 'Criterion for formal integrability'.
Hilbert published 'Über den Begriff der Klasse von Differentialgleichungen' in Math. Ann. 73 (1912), pp. 95–108, on underdetermined differential systems.
Hilbert's 1912 paper is linked to old problems about explicitly describing solutions of underdetermined systems, which are now studied as differential flatness in control theory.
Compatibility criteria for overdetermined PDE systems are still a research subject today, including the Kruglikov–Lychagin brackets approach.

triage.why: The note asks for a general criterion that a PDE system is 'really determined'. That is the problem formal integrability and involution theory (Riquier–Janet, Cartan–Kähler, Spencer) was built to solve, and it gives such criteria at least in the analytic category. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. No source links this specific diary entry to any of these later results, so 'solved' means the problem was settled in general by later theory, not that someone answered Hilbert's note. I could not confirm which exact system was on the page, so the match is a reasonable identification rather than a certain one. Related work on compatibility criteria and flatness, the modern form of Hilbert's 1912 'class' question, is still active.
